Over the years Owlie has been privileged to set dovra on paper many thousands of words,
either for publication in the news media or for the judiciary to review in the privacy of their
chambers. The former were articles written under pressure to meet deadlines for the morning
edition of the local newspaper. The latter, in contrast, were considered affidavits or briefs
handed up to the bench to substantiate represented positions with interpretations of the law in
specific cases.
It has been many years since Owlie has engaged in the first of these divergent styles ofwriting
and could rightfully call himself "an ink-stained wretch," an epithet so often used to designate
those pursuing the joumahstic profession. Hence it has been some time since Owlie has been
both the recipient ofgenerous accolades from certain readers and the target ofoutrageous arrows
from others.
For the last four years your scribe has been given the opportunity of returning to this earlier
calling. It has been his objective to make The Diamond of Psi Upsilon more interesting for its
readers. In the course of his efforts he has wandered extensively in subject matter, yet always
dedicated in one way or another to the betterment of Psi Upsilon. The gamut ofhis meanderings
has ranged far and wide, but consistently endeavoring to move in a constructive direction. These
have been carefully weighed excursions into the world of journalism that he knew "way back
when."
Unlike the "old days," however, comments from our readers have been few and far between.
Those reactions we have received invariably have been on the side of qualified praise. In one
instance an alumnus far removed from the fraternity scene was inspired to join the growing army
of loyal Psi U alumni who contribute annually of their resources toward the goals and causes of
our Fraternity.
In recent column Owlie ventured into a new area of financial support available to our alumni
who wish to assure the perpetuation of Psi Upsilon down through the years. It was recognized
that many of our brothers may find it difficult to give of their substance during their lifetime, for
one reason or another. An alternative was presented of providing for Psi Upsilon after one's
departure from this world a gift which could be larger and even more helpful to the Executive
Council and the Fraternity at large than an annual contribution. Your writer has been involved in
lengthy discussions of this possibility with alumni of his own Chapter. All concur that here,
indeed, is a means of assuring the perpetuation of the Chapter as well.
Since proposing that alternative to the great body of Psi U's readership, Owlie has been
surprised to have received but one response. It came in the form ofan expression ofregret by one
in this same Chapter that he would be unable to include a sizeable bequest to the Chapter in his
Last Will and Testament. The objection stemmed from his wife, who justifiably felt that her
husband should provide first for her, in the event she survived him, with the possibility that she
might have to face later on the heavy expense of a long illness. Each with whom the alumnus
shared his decision agreed with the soundness of his wife's position, but a way out of this impasse
was suggested.
Legal beagles in whom the alumnus confided proposed that funds which a donor wished to
bequeath to such organizations as his Chapter, the Fraternity, and/or his college or university
could be placed in a trust. The income from this trust would be directed to the widow, if she
survived her husband, and she should have the right to invade the principal of the trust, ff
necessary. Upon her demise the trust could be terminated, with the principal distributed to the
stipulated beneficiaries in accordance vwth the original trust agreement.
The purpose of repeating this suggestion of an earher column that gifts to Psi Upsilon after
death be considered by our alumni membership, of course, is to impress this means of aiding the
Fraternity upon our readers and to elicit further responses. Here is an ideal way to translate our
loyalty into tangible form by augmenting Psi Upsilon's limited endowment funds. OwHe truly
hopes that many will take this suggestion to heart and initiate steps toward its realization.

Conventions serve as the primary

Fraternity, it must be remembered. In
cluded in resolutions enacted this year

(1) The term ofthe Psi Upsilon Fellow's
appointment to be extended from twelve

(2) The title ofthe Psi Upsilon Fellow to

(3) A final budget for the fiscal year

hoped that the col

ing hand.
Home of "The Raven"
The Delta of Psi Upsilon and the City of
Philadelphia are at odds regarding the
birthplace of Edgar Allan Poe's The
Raven. A federal grant of $469,000 re
cently was approved for renovating a
Philadelphia row house where it is
claimed that the author, generally cred
ited with perfecting the short story form
of writing, lived from 1842 to 1844 and
composed the immortal poem.
But scholars who have researched his
toric Greenwich Village, the center of
New York City's artistic and literary ac
tivities, attest to The Raven having been
completed in the building now owned by
New York University and leased to the
Delta Chapter. Its first reading is re
ported to have taken place at a literary
soiree in the Waverly Place home of a
Miss Wild, one of Poe's benefactors. The
Delta Alumni Association has applied for
the designation of the Chapter House as a
National Historic Landmark. In light of
the considerable funds already expended
both by the University and the Delta in
reno\ating 85 West 3rd Street, the Gov
ernment could preserve Psi Upsilon's
claimed site of Edgar Allan Poe's greatest
writing at an appreciable sa\ ing!

THETA
1833
Although the Theta is small in numbers
this year, a revived spirit of unity and
purpose has strengthened the under
graduate brotherhood. With thirteen
Brothers studying abroad or following
other interests, there remain but eigh
teen actives to carry on.
As of this writing, the Theta is looking
forward to a successful rush under the
able leadership of Brother David Finnigan '80.
The physical condition of the House is
comparatively good, as the Brothers
worked hard to get things in order before
classes began.
Our financial situation, although not
envious, is improving. The dedication
and hard work of the Chapter Trustees
has enabled the Theta to begin slowly to
move out of debt. New projects this year
include publishing a newsletter, which
hopefully will encourage greater alumni
interest.
Brother Paul Matz '79 has won our es
teem by being chosen a Nott Scholar. Psi
U's continue to be active in intramurals,
as well as in varsity sports. The Chapter is
represented on the varsity soccer, wres
tling, swimming, lacrosse, rugby, and
baseball teams. Other Brothers are active
with the Glee Club, newspaper, and the
College theatre.

1837

1 lodge room, and new furniture are just a
I few of the additions our new House acI
quired last summer. Our library is grow

The Delta Chapter was very proud to

Sandy Scharf also is Treasurer for the
Student Government, and Mike Walsh is

fraternities to join the Interfraternity
Council at N.Y. U. This year's President is

are Mike Walsh and Jon Spaet '78.
Finally, the pledge class for the first

the Brothers of the Delta are making
every effort this year to match last year's
significant accomplishments.
Michael J. Walsh '79
Secretary
GAMMA
1841
Life at the Gamma Chapter has never
been better. Under the direction of our
first semester President, Scott Alfgren,
the sixty members of Psi Upsilon at
Amherst have continued to form a very
close-knit group.
Twenty-five of these members are Oc
tober initiates of the sophomore class,
twenty-three of whom indicated a desire
to live in the House. In order to accom
modate this delegation and the usual con
tingent of upperclassmen, it was neces
sary to increase the size of the House by
one. This move most probably is a tem
porary action; next year we will return to
our usual thirty-one "live-in" members.
The Gamma Chapter was very active in
varsity sports during the fall. Notably,
Brother Bob Sternberg was a halfback for
the Amherst Lord Jeffs and picked up 64

Bowdoin Polar Bears. Gamma members
also participated on varsity soccer and
crew teams. Most of us, however, have
been preparing for the winter sports, with
close to twenty members involved on var
sity teams such as swimming, basketball
and squash.
Our House is in top shape. With the
financial assistance of our Corporation we
have bought additional furniture for our
living room.
In summary, spirits at the Gamma are
exceedingly high!
Theodore Sizer, II 7.9

1976-77 Annual Giving Results Best Yet;
Record Breaker Seen as Pointing Trend
The remarkable response of Psi Upsilon alumni to the Frater
nity's annual appeal for financial support in recent years has
been the key factor in keeping undergraduate dues and mem
bership fees among the lowest of all fraternities. Annual Giving
now finances more than one-half of the Executive Council's
operating expenses.
In 1976-77 contributions totaling $54,196 were received,
toppingthepreviousyear's record high by $4,000. A significant
feature of this continuing gain was the growing number of
alumni who accepted leadership responsibility, an increase
from 259 to 335 Brothers. In all 1,774 alumni gave an average
of $30.55 between July, 1976 and June, 1977, up from
$27.78 the preceding year, with equally welcome donations
ranging from $5 to $1,000.
This represents a participation of 11.4 percent of the alumni
last year, and it is in this area that the greatest potential for
further gains exists. We are advised that an
average gift of
$2.50 per alumnus with good address is considered excellent.
Psi Upsilon's average of $3.49 in 1976-77 is believed to have
been the highest in the fraternity world.
Years of consecutive giving are shown in parentheses after
the name and class of donors in the acknowledgment lists
which follow. Names in italics are leadership contributors.
Tables of relative achievement by Chapter will appear in the
next issue.
The Executive Council is deeply and profoundly grateful for
the loyal and generous backing of Psi Upsilon alumni. The need
is never-ending, of course, and in fact increases each year as
costs continue to escalate. Hence even greater heights must be
attained in 1977-78.

1970
The spirit at the Gamma Tau reached a
new high during the fall with the visit of
Mike Huffman, the Psi U Field Director,
during fall rush. With eleven aggressive
Brothers returning this year, the Chapter
launched its most successful formal rush
since its inception seven years ago. Rush
Chairman Joe DiNunno '79 led the cam
paign to bring the Gamma Tau member
ship to an all-time high.
Our newest delegation consists of elev
en men from the Class of 1981: Joseph
Barrett, Steven Cline, Robert Davis,
Donnie Figuett, Jeffrey Fracas, Allen
Massey, Vincent Parente, Darrell Peet,
Mario Ricozzi, Charles Roan, and Donald
Zyriek.
On the same day as our pledge cere
mony, the brotherhood also initiated
three new Little Sisters of the Gamma
Tau: Gayle Breor, Jane Carter and Janice
Saraceno.
Having won both the Psi U trophy and
the Georgia Tech trophy for academics in
1976-77, the Brothers and pledges are
facing the challenge of repeating their
high standing. Led by Brothers C. Henry
Hoeft '78 and Jim Jones '79, who achieved
perfect 4.0 grade point averages last
spring, the Chapter expects to meet that
challenge.
Our major event of the fall quarter was
the Georgia Tech Homecoming vs. Duke
University on October 29. This time was
chosen to provide the backdrop for the
annual Founders' Day Dinner, -with the
Chi Delta Chapter driving down to help
us celebrate.
Joseph N. DiNunno, Jr. '79

1973
The Chi Delta, under the leadership of
President Bob Pillote '78 is enjoying an
active and promising year. Chapter reno
vations have continued, as we have added
some finishing touches to our refurbished
bar room and have completed the con
struction of two new benches for the out
side of our section.
Our Social Chairman, Dan Tyukody
'78, was responsible for an elaborate fall
social schedule, including parties on vari
ous themes, such as "The Newly Nostal
gic Sixties," "green goddess,
"
and "a
night at the races," not to mention a visit
to the Gamma Tau Chapter on the
weekend of the Duke football game
against Georgia Tech.

brotherhood.

The Executive Council has responded
to numerous inquiries by authorizing the
preparation of an updated directory of all
living alumni of Psi Upsilon. Scheduled
for publication in December, this
eighteenth edition will be the first direc
tory printed since 1955, nearly a quarter
of a century ago.
The Bernard C. Harris Publishing
Company, Inc. of New York has been
selected as the official pubfisher after a
thorough review of this firm's extensive
experience and success. Recognized as
the oldest and largest exclusive publisher
of alumni directories in the world, Harris
Publishing has completed over the past
thirty years more than 200 alumni direc
tories for colleges, universities, second
ary schools, and fraternal organizations.
This extensive project will be under
taken at virtually no cost to the Frater
nity. Harris Publishing has contracted to
compile, publish, and market the direc
tory for our more than 17,000 alumni,
financing the operation solely through the
sale of individual directory copies. Nor
will Psi Upsilon benefit financially from
the directory sales; purchases should not
be considered as a contribution. But the
Fraternity will derive substantial benefit
from the updated addresses and other
valuable information obtained.
The main body of the directory will
consist of an alphabetical listing of all
alumni, with each entry to include name,
chapter, class, college or university,
home address and telephone, and busiDirectory Underway
ness or professional information, includ
ing address and telephone. Two complete
indexes of all alumni, one arranged geo
graphically by towns within states and the
other alphabetically within each Chapter,
will follow the main listings, providing
ready references.
This updated material will be derived
from brief questionnaires to be mailed
from the Fraternity Office in April and
May to all alumni with known addresses.
Since the completeness and accuracy of
the directory coverage depends upon the
response of the alumni, all are urged to fill
out the questionnaire carefully and legi
bly, returning it to Psi Upsilon at their
earliest convenience.
During the months of July and August,
once this data has been compiled, all
alumni will be contacted by telephone for
verification of the information to be
printed in the directory. At that time, and
at that time only, they will be invited to
purchase a hard-bound or soft-bound
copy. The Bernard C. Harris Company
will publish only enough directories to fill
these pre-publication orders, and no one
except alumni will be permitted to pur
chase copies.
The Executive Council urges the full
cooperation of Psi Upsilon's entire mem
bership, in the firm conviction that this
undertaking constitutes a significant
service and an important milestone. .\n\
